title: Data-driven clinical decision trees and generative topographic mapping to guide stroke rehabilitation program allocation
content:
by Dimitrios Sokratis Komaris, Panagiotis Anagnostou, Spiros Nikolopoulos, Dimitrios Tsaopoulos, Anna Guillen-Sola, Esther Duarte, Ryan A. A. Bellfield, Sandra Ortega-Martorell, Ivan Olier, Ioannis Kompatsiaris

Background

Early and timely admission to post-stroke rehabilitation remains a key determinant of optimal functional recovery. In this study, we present a structured framework for the development and evaluation of multivariable prediction models and Classification and Regression Tree (CART) decision-support tools to guide patient allocation across diverse subacute rehabilitation settings.

Methods

We have constructed a heterogeneous synthetic dataset of 700 stroke patients characterized by 49 demographic, clinical, and functional variables derived from multiple, literature-reported, statistical distributions of patient populations. Subsequently, the dataset was independently annotated by an expert panel of clinicians, who assigned each stroke patient to one of seven rehabilitation programs ranging from home-based to high-intensity hospital-based care (target outcome). Feature importance analysis identified cognitive function status, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, age, presence of early seizures, and alcohol consumption as the most influential predictors of rehabilitation program allocation. Six supervised classifiers were then trained to predict rehabilitation program allocation, along with shallow CARTs of different depths. Internal evaluation used 200 repetitions of stratified ten-fold cross-validation, with metrics calculated from pooled out-of-fold predictions and summarized as mean and standard deviation.

Results

In internal evaluation against the expert-assigned labels, the XGBoost and the best-performing CART model achieved mean accuracies of 0.832 and 0.847 and balanced accuracies of 0.381 and 0.393, respectively. Both exceeded the institutional benchmark, which achieved accuracy of 0.753 and balanced accuracy of 0.325. Key predictors included cognitive function status, NIHSS score, age, presence of early seizures, and alcohol consumption. In addition, Generative Topographic Mapping (GTM) facilitated the exploration of patient relationships within different prediction models that may help distinguish clusters with similar phenotypes, i.e., patient groups with shared clinical characteristics. It further enabled the visual comparison of stroke rehabilitation program predictions across models (e.g., baseline versus CART model). This allowed for assessment of program recommendations by the developed models in transparent and meaningful ways, and the identification of patient characteristics influencing divergent model decisions.

Conclusions

This study demonstrates the feasibility of developing and evaluating multivariable prediction models for rehabilitation program allocation using an openly shared and expert-annotated dataset. This framework offers a transparent and adaptable foundation for developing bespoke, data-driven decision-support systems in stroke rehabilitation. Ultimately, the proposed approach promotes interpretable, context-sensitive, and individualized rehabilitation planning adaptable to varying clinical resources and practices.
